why: The plan explains how sunlight pushes the tail before it gives the viewer a reason to care, and its stakes line is abstract ("matters for science"); no twist is declared to excuse it (attention 8, 10).

review.logline: A comet's tail leads it away from the Sun because sunlight and a wind from the Sun push it, not because it trails behind.
review.synopsis: Sunlight presses on a comet's dust and gas; a comet leaves the Sun tail first; sunlight is too weak to explain the gas tail; Biermann proposes a wind from the Sun and Mariner 2 measures it; the opening comet is seen again. Nothing says what the wind does to anyone.

flags.problem: The plan explains the push of sunlight before it gives any reason to care, and its stakes line says only that understanding this matters for science: no consequence the viewer can picture, and no twist declared to excuse it.
flags.fix: Open on a consequence the viewer can picture before the mechanism: the same wind that bends this tail put Quebec's grid out for nine hours in March 1989.

first_minute.promise_match: From the plan (no script yet): section 1 opens on how sunlight pushes a comet's dust and gas, then a comet leaving the Sun tail first, the subject the title promised.
first_minute.question_and_stakes: From the plan: why the tail leads, but section 1 explains the push before it says why anyone should care, and the stakes line says only that it matters for science.

problems.problem: Section 1 explains how sunlight pushes the tail before the viewer hears any consequence they can picture, and the stakes line says only that it matters for science.
problems.fix: Open section 1 on the 1989 Quebec blackout, a storm in the same wind that bends the tail, before the push is explained.
